profiles.meeting_scenario: The Michigan Access to Justice Commission is preparing a replication package for other state court systems based on its completed quality-improvement program that embedded legal-help navigators and court-staff feedback loops in district courts handling eviction and family-law matters. An internal review has stalled the package because the newly drafted ex post program theory draws heavily on what staff learned during implementation, while the formal grant closeout file presents a cleaner, narrower description of the program. The meeting is a troubleshooting session between program strategy and legal/compliance leads to diagnose why the theory update is not clearing review and to decide how to revise it without losing the lessons learned from Michigan. Agenda: identify the source of the mismatch, determine whether the problem is the narrative, the supporting documentation, or the packaging for transfer to other jurisdictions, and agree on the next revision path. Expected outcome: a shared action plan for revising the theory memo and supporting materials before circulation to funders and partner courts.

members.name: Leah Benton
members.role: Director of Program Strategy, Michigan Access to Justice Commission
members.expertise: Court operations improvement, legal-aid service design, implementation learning
members.background: Former supervising attorney at a statewide legal-aid organization who led the original Michigan court-site rollout and later managed the program's replication toolkit.
members.private_state: She wants the updated theory to capture the real causal mechanisms that made the Michigan effort work, especially the informal feedback loops and local adaptations that never fit neatly into the grant narrative. She is concerned that legal review will sanitize the theory into a generic training-and-referral model that other jurisdictions cannot actually reproduce.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues refer to 'the record,' they naturally include internal implementation artifacts such as coaching notes, site debriefs, and staff-maintained change logs.
When people say 'the Michigan sites' or 'the pilot courts,' they usually mean the three original demonstration courts where most iteration occurred.
Implementation experience includes informal adjustments made by navigators, clerks, and program staff during rollout, even if those adjustments were never written into a formal amendment.
A program theory is transferable only if it captures the tacit operating conditions and recurring troubleshooting routines that produced results on the ground.

members.name: Omar Shah
members.role: Associate General Counsel for Grants and Administrative Compliance
members.expertise: Grant compliance, public-sector documentation, administrative risk in court programs
members.background: Former state assistant attorney general and court administrator who now reviews externally funded access-to-justice initiatives for consistency with grant files, board materials, and public reporting obligations.
members.private_state: He wants the replication package to survive scrutiny from funders, auditors, and court partners without creating the impression that the Commission ran a materially different program from the one described in the official file. He is worried that a richly descriptive ex post theory could be read as admitting undocumented deviations or unsupported causal claims.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say 'the record,' they mean the formal, citable file: grant applications, approved workplans, amendments, board minutes, and closeout reports.
When people refer to 'the Michigan pilot courts,' they mean all six courts listed in the program's closeout appendix, not just the original demonstration cohort.
Implementation experience that can anchor a public-facing theory should be limited to activities and refinements that were within the approved grant scope and time period.
A program theory is transferable if another jurisdiction can adopt the package without needing extensive extra legal vetting or creating inconsistencies with the official Michigan file.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the revised theory needs to 'match the record' or be 'in the record.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the accumulated implementation archive, including coaching notes, staff debriefs, site-visit memos, and internal change logs that explain how the program actually evolved.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the formal administrative file that can be cited externally: approved grant documents, filed progress reports, amendments, and closeout materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal settings, 'the record' is a familiar phrase that usually goes unexamined because both speakers assume the institutional meaning is obvious; each hears a sensible version of the phrase and has no immediate reason to probe.

misalignment_points.topic: Which courts are 'the Michigan pilot sites'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the Michigan sites,' 'the pilot courts,' or 'what happened in Michigan.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is mainly thinking of the three original demonstration courts in Kent, Genesee, and Washtenaw Counties, where the iterative quality-improvement work was most intensive.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of all six courts named in the closeout appendix, including the three later-adopting courts that implemented a more standardized version.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both groupings are legitimately called the Michigan pilot in different internal documents, so the phrase feels settled and shared even though each person is silently drawing evidence from a different set of sites.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the updated theory should reflect 'implementation experience.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the informal weekly troubleshooting calls, clerk workarounds, navigator-script changes, and court-specific workflow adjustments that emerged during rollout.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes only the implementation steps and refinements that were within the approved workplan and grant period, excluding undocumented local improvisations from the core description.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds methodologically responsible and commonplace, so neither person feels a need to specify its boundary; both assume they are merely endorsing a standard ex post update.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to make the theory 'transferable'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the revised package needs to be 'transferable' to other jurisdictions.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks transferability means giving future adopters enough operational detail about enabling conditions, decision rules, and feedback routines to recreate the Michigan mechanism.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks transferability means packaging the model so it can be reused elsewhere without triggering legal ambiguity, bespoke compliance review, or questions about inconsistency with the original file.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Transferability is a positive, high-level goal that both sincerely endorse, but the standard for having achieved it differs in a second-order way that only matters later during drafting and review.

turns.inner_thought: This keeps getting flattened into a generic training-and-referral package. If other courts only get the cleaned-up version, they will miss the actual mechanism from the three original demonstration courts: the constant local adjustment, the feedback loops, the way staff learned week by week. Transferable, to me, means someone else can recreate those operating conditions, not just copy a slide deck.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. From where I sit, the package keeps stalling because the ex post theory still doesn't explain why what happened in Michigan is actually transferable. Right now it reads as if the model is basically navigator onboarding plus referral points, and that leaves out too much of what made the pilot courts work.

turns.inner_thought: The problem is not that the lessons are unusable; it's that the latest memo sounds broader and more causal than the formal file supports. If we circulate language that appears to describe a materially different program from the grant applications, amendments, reports, board materials, and closeout appendix, we create avoidable risk. Transferable means other jurisdictions can pick this up without inviting questions from funders or counsel.
turns.utterance: I don't think legal review is objecting to the idea that lessons from Michigan should be usable elsewhere. The sticking point is that the newest draft reads differently from the record. If we're going to make the package transferable, we need a theory that lines up with what is already in the file and doesn't create confusion for funders or court partners.

turns.inner_thought: He keeps saying 'the file,' but the real story is in the implementation archive: coaching notes, weekly debriefs, change logs, site memos. And when I say the Michigan sites, I'm thinking of Kent, Genesee, and Washtenaw, where the troubleshooting loops actually shaped the model. That's the implementation experience that matters.
turns.utterance: I hear that, but if the theory is really going to reflect implementation experience from the Michigan sites, then it has to include the weekly troubleshooting loops with court staff. Those weren't side conversations. They were part of how the pilot courts figured out what would actually hold in a live docket environment.

turns.inner_thought: I'm not opposed to including iterative work, but it needs to be supportable across all six courts named in the closeout appendix, not just the more intensively supported early adopters. And whatever goes in the theory has to be anchored in the formal record, not in informal notes that were never part of the external file.
turns.utterance: I'm not against that category of material. My concern is that if we include it, we need to be able to support it across the pilot courts and anchor it in the record. Otherwise the theory starts to look selective, and that's where review gets uneasy.

turns.inner_thought: The draft keeps centering the most legible thing—training—because it's easy to point to. But in practice the core work was all the unglamorous adjustments navigators, clerks, and supervisors made together: intake timing, referral routing, script edits, handoff points. If we call training the intervention, we are misdescribing the implementation experience.
turns.utterance: Exactly, and that's why I think the current draft is off. It treats navigator training as the intervention, when in practice the implementation experience was the continuous adjustment of filing and referral workflows with clerks. Training mattered, obviously, but it wasn't the whole engine.

turns.inner_thought: She may be right that the program matured through ongoing adjustment, but I have to keep the public-facing theory from implying undocumented deviations or unsupported causal claims. If we frame this as a general implementation feature, consistent with the official materials, maybe we can preserve some of it without turning the memo into an admission that the real program differed from the approved one.
turns.utterance: I can see that. Continuous adjustment may still belong in the theory, but it has to be framed in a way that remains transferable and does not outrun what the official materials show. If it reads like a separate intervention layer that never appears in the record, that's where I start to worry.

turns.inner_thought: What future adopters need is a candid section on the enabling conditions from the original courts: manager check-ins, script changes, regular troubleshooting routines, the little operating rules everyone learned. That's what made the model function. If we omit those conditions, we are exporting a shell.
turns.utterance: What if we add a section on the conditions that made the Michigan sites work? I'm thinking of the court-manager check-ins, the script changes, and the things that emerged during implementation. That would let us explain the model more honestly without turning the whole memo into a blow-by-blow narrative.

turns.inner_thought: A conditions section could help if it is written as a statewide Michigan model that reflects all six sites, especially the later courts that followed a more standardized approach. I don't want a replication package that quietly generalizes from only part of the pilot and then gets presented as the Michigan experience overall.
turns.utterance: In principle, yes. I would just want that section to read as a Michigan model, not as a story drawn from only part of the pilot courts. If we're saying these are the conditions for transferability, they need to be framed at the level of what happened in Michigan, not as a subset case study.

turns.inner_thought: We actually do have support for this if people will count the implementation archive as part of the record. The debriefs and coaching logs show how the model evolved and what staff kept solving for. That's exactly the evidence base for the theory update. I need to get that material in front of him without making it sound like I'm introducing something foreign.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the answer is to attach a few examples from site debriefs and coaching logs so the revised theory is clearly in the record and shows how the model evolved through implementation experience. That might make the language feel less abstract and less like we're asserting lessons without support.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want informal materials appended as if they carry the same status as the closeout file, but a crosswalk could let us separate supportable theory language from illustrative transfer tools. If we map each theory element to the closeout appendix and package the rest carefully, we may be able to preserve her goals while keeping the file consistent and defensible.
turns.utterance: I think the cleanest next step is a crosswalk. Let's map the revised theory against the closeout appendix and the transfer package, and then we can see where each point is supportable, where it needs softer wording, and what belongs in implementation guidance rather than the core memo. If we do that well, we should be able to land a version that's both supportable and transferable.
